body.statement: Fix \(c>0\) and \(v\in\{\mathrm w,+\}\). Under \(P\in\operatorname{ri}(C_c^v)\), the projected empirical law \(\widetilde P_n\) is eventually attainable almost surely and \(L_c^v(\widetilde P_n)\to L_c^v(P)\) and \(U_c^v(\widetilde P_n)\to U_c^v(P)\) almost surely.
body.justification: Convex endpoint values are relatively continuous at fixed-slope relative-interior attainable laws, and affine-hull projection preserves empirical convergence.
body.gap: The proof gives no boundary continuity and no joint consistency when \(c\) varies through one.
body.consumer: It justifies only pointwise fixed-slope plug-in endpoint estimation in the stated interior regime.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(c>0\) and \(v\in\{\mathrm w,+\}\), and abbreviate \(C=C_c^v\).  First construct a strictly positive law \(P^\star\in C\): take \(\mu\) to be unit mass at \(u=1\), set \(h_x(1)=1/2\) for both \(x\), and set \(g_{xy}(z,1)=1/2\) for every \(x,y,z\in B\).  These kernels belong even to \(\mathcal M_+(c)\), and the logit response probabilities are strictly positive.  Hence
\[
 P^\star(x,y,z,w)=\frac14p_x(y,1)p_z(w,1)>0 \tag{1}
\]
for all sixteen cells.

Suppose \(P\in\operatorname{ri}(C)\).  If a cell coordinate \(P_j\) were zero, then \(P-P^\star\) would be parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\), and the relative-interior ball would contain
\[
 P+\epsilon(P-P^\star)
\]
for every sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\).  Its \(j\)-th coordinate would be \(-\epsilon P_j^\star<0\), contradicting \(C\subseteq\Delta^{15}\).  Thus every cell of \(P\) is positive.

Let
\[
 \mathcal O=\{Q\in\Delta^{15}:Q_j>0\text{ for all sixteen cells }j\},
 \qquad D=C\cap\mathcal O.
\]
The set \(D\) is convex.  Indeed, take \(Q_0,Q_1\in D\), choose attainable effects \(d_0,d_1\), and let \(z_j\in\mathcal F_c^v(Q_j,d_j)\), whose existence follows from \(\mathrm{thm{:}exact\text{-}feedback\text{-}cone}\).  For \(0\le\lambda\le1\), all lift equalities are affine and every PSD block is preserved by convex combination, so
\[
 \lambda z_0+(1-\lambda)z_1
 \in\mathcal F_c^v\bigl(\lambda Q_0+(1-\lambda)Q_1,
 \lambda d_0+(1-\lambda)d_1\bigr). \tag{2}
\]
The mixed law has positive cells, and the reverse implication of the same theorem places it in \(C\), hence in \(D\).

Moreover, \(P\in\operatorname{ri}(D)\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\).  The relative-interior assumption supplies \(\delta_0>0\) such that the relative ball of radius \(\delta_0\) around \(P\) lies in \(C\).  Positivity of all coordinates of \(P\) supplies \(\delta_1>0\) such that the corresponding relative ball lies in \(\mathcal O\).  The ball of radius \(\min\{\delta_0,\delta_1\}\) lies in \(D\), and therefore \(\operatorname{aff}(D)=\operatorname{aff}(C)\).

The lower value function is convex on \(D\).  For \(Q_0,Q_1\in D\) and \(\epsilon>0\), choose \(d_j\) in the fiber over \(Q_j\) with
\[
 d_j<L_c^v(Q_j)+\epsilon.
\]
The mixture argument (2) gives
\[
 L_c^v\bigl(\lambda Q_0+(1-\lambda)Q_1\bigr)
 \le \lambda L_c^v(Q_0)+(1-\lambda)L_c^v(Q_1)+\epsilon.
\]
Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) proves convexity.  Choosing effects within \(\epsilon\) of the two suprema and reversing the inequality proves that \(U_c^v\) is concave, so \(-U_c^v\) is convex.  Both are finite on \(D\) by \(\mathrm{thm{:}fixed\text{-}slope\text{-}endpoints}\).  Extend each of \(L_c^v\) and \(-U_c^v\) by \(+\infty\) off \(D\).  These extensions are proper convex functions with domain \(D\).  Applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}relative\text{-}interior\text{-}convex\text{-}continuity}\) at \(P\in\operatorname{ri}(D)\) proves that \(L_c^v\) and \(U_c^v\) are continuous at \(P\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\).

It remains to control the empirical argument.  For one cell let \(Z_i\) be its indicator, put \(p=\mathbb E Z_i\), and set \(W_i=Z_i-p\).  Independence and centering imply that every term in the fourth-moment expansion vanishes unless each index occurs at least twice.  Since \(|W_i|\le1\),
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nW_i\right)^4\right]
 =\frac{n\mathbb E[W_1^4]+3n(n-1)\{\mathbb E[W_1^2]\}^2}{n^4}
 \le\frac{3}{n^2}. \tag{3}
\]
For every \(\epsilon>0\), the pointwise fourth-power bound gives
\[
 \Pr\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nW_i\right|>\epsilon\right)
 \le\frac{3}{\epsilon^4n^2}. \tag{4}
\]
The probability of at least one such deviation after time \(N\) is at most \(3\epsilon^{-4}\sum_{n\ge N}n^{-2}\), which tends to zero.  Taking the intersection of the resulting probability-one events over \(\epsilon=1/k\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), and over the sixteen cells proves
\[
 \widehat P_n\longrightarrow P\qquad\text{almost surely}. \tag{5}
\]

Set \(A=\operatorname{aff}(C)\).  This is a closed affine subspace of the finite-dimensional cell space, and \(P\in A\).  Orthogonal projection onto \(A\) is nonexpansive, so
\[
 \|\widetilde P_n-P\|_2\le\|\widehat P_n-P\|_2. \tag{6}
\]
Equations (5)--(6) give \(\widetilde P_n\to P\) almost surely.  The relative ball above therefore contains \(\widetilde P_n\) eventually almost surely, so \(\widetilde P_n\in D\subseteq C\) eventually.  Relative continuity now yields
\[
 L_c^v(\widetilde P_n)\longrightarrow L_c^v(P),
 \qquad
 U_c^v(\widetilde P_n)\longrightarrow U_c^v(P)
\]
almost surely.  The proof keeps \(c\) fixed and uses the relative-interior ball essentially; it gives neither boundary continuity nor joint consistency through varying \(c\).
